title: Final Destination 2
full_review:
Exploiting violence to make a quick buck is the name of the game for "Final Destination 2" (New Line).

The gross sequel to the movie from 2000 simply repeats the premise: A college student has a premonition of a lethal accident so saves herself and others, only to find "Death" is stalking each of them.

Driving onto a highway with three pals, Kimberly (A.J. Cook) has a sudden terrifying premonition of a logging truck losing its timber load and a multicar pileup resulting. Screeching to a halt at the entrance ramp to save herself and the cars behind, she tries to explain her vision to a police trooper (Michael Landes) when the explosive accident happens, killing those in the truck's wake.

Exactly a year earlier, a plane crashed but a similar premonition saved several friends from boarding. Soon after, each survivor died with the exception of Clear (Ali Larter), who checked herself into a psychiatric institute's padded room for protection. When the highway disaster's first survivor dies the next day in a freak impaling, Clear comes out in the open to help Kimberly and the cop warn the others to be extra careful. They fail -- or to put it more accurately, the film succeeds -- in wallowing in one gross death scene after another.

Director David R. Ellis simply strings together a series of individual demises that are spectacularly horrible. The characters in the story only exist to be mutilated into nonexistence. With constant high-tech, computer-generated special effects, the movie is quickly reduced to graphic and gory killings, a parade of in-your-face immolations, explosions, impalings, decapitations, bisections and dismemberments. There is not so much suspense as there is a bored sense of dread: OK, who's next?

The stomach-churning visuals end on a smug, life-is-cheap sight gag at a barbecue where everyone breathes a sigh of relief that the bloodletting is finally over, only to have the barbecue grill explode and a boy's bloody arm land on his mom's dinner plate.

Because of excessive, gory violence, some recreational drug use, a flash of nudity and intermittent profanity and rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
